question: Joey and Chloe and their daughter Zoe all have the same birthday. Joey is \(1\) year older than Chloe, and Zoe is exactly \(1\) year old today. Today is the first of the \(9\) birthdays on which Chloe’s age will be an integral multiple of Zoe’s age. What will be the sum of the two digits of Joey’s age the next time his age is a multiple of Zoe’s age?
solution:
Because their age differences stay fixed, the birthdays when one age is a multiple of another can be described using divisors.

Let Chloe be \(n\) years old today. In \(y\) years, where \(y\) is a nonnegative integer, her age divided by Zoe's age will be
\[
\frac{n+y}{1+y}=1+\frac{n-1}{1+y}.
\]
This is an integer exactly when \(1+y\) divides \(n-1\). Each positive divisor gives exactly one such birthday, so \(n-1\) has exactly \(9\) positive divisors.

If an integer has prime factorization \(\prod r_i^{e_i}\), its divisor count is \(\prod(e_i+1)\), since each divisor independently chooses an exponent from \(0\) through \(e_i\). The only ways to obtain \(9\) are therefore
\[
n-1=p^8
\quad\text{or}\quad
n-1=p^2r^2,
\]
where \(p,r\) are distinct primes in the second case.

The question specifies that Joey's age at the requested later birthday has two digits. His current age is smaller, so \(n-1<100\). But \(p^8\ge 2^8=256\). Also, the smallest product of two distinct primes is \(2\cdot3=6\), and every other such product is at least \(10\). Thus the only possibility below \(100\) is
\[
n-1=2^2\cdot3^2=36.
\]
Chloe is consequently \(37\) today, and Joey is \(38\).

For Joey, the corresponding age ratio is
\[
\frac{38+y}{1+y}=1+\frac{37}{1+y}.
\]
Since \(37\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(37\). These give \(y=0\) and \(y=36\). At the next qualifying birthday, Joey will be \(38+36=74\), whose digit sum is
\[
7+4=\boxed{11}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
